JOHANNESBURG, South Africa (CNN) -- The atmosphere was tense in Cape Town on Friday after xenophobic violence that has left more than 40 dead in Johannesburg spread to South Africa's largest city. Immigrants from Mozambique line up in Primrose, South Africa, to board buses back home. Clashes overnight resulted in one death and 15 arrests and the evacuations of 420 foreign nationals, a police official in Cape Town said. "Crowds of people went on a rampage, looting and carrying out acts of violence," said Cape Town Police Superintendent Billy Jones. They were charged with public violence and are to appear in court Monday. One foreign national, a Somali, died when he was run over by a vehicle as he tried to escape the angry crowds, Jones said. Twelve people suffered minor injuries. He said Friday was tense but calm, with state and local police stationed throughout the area. Jack Bloom of the opposition party Democratic Alliance told CNN on Friday that government troops were helping police ward off violence in Johannesburg. Aid workers and volunteers were providing tents, food and supplies at the police stations. Bloom estimated that about 2,000 foreigners had sought haven at those locations. It was the first violence in the coastal city since a wave of xenophobia began about two weeks ago in Johannesburg, resulting in at least 42 deaths. The foreign nationals were transported from the city after angry crowds formed at a public meeting seeking to calm tensions, Jones told CNN. They were being housed at community centers and churches. The attacks in South Africa have forced thousands of immigrants to flee, prompting neighboring Mozambique to declare a state of emergency on Friday. Desperate stories of those fleeing violence . The country's Foreign Minister Oldemiro Baloi said the decision was taken after about 10,000 Mozambicans fled from South Africa. CNN's Robyn Curnow reported long lines of people -- including many from Zimbabwe and Mozambique -- waiting for buses in Johannesburg to take them home. Bloom, from Gauteng province, which includes Johannesburg, said the attacks on foreigners who fled to South Africa for a better life has become a "humanitarian crisis." South African President Thabo Mbeki has approved the deployment of the army to help stop the attacks, which have drawn condemnation from South African officials and other African leaders. About 28,000 people have been displaced by the violence, Hangwani Malaudzi, a spokesman for the Ministry of Safety and Security said. And more than 400 have been arrested for crimes ranging from murder, to causing a public disturbance, he said. The country has also seen a disturbing throwback to the 1980s apartheid-era lynching tactic of "necklacing," which was widely used in the townships at the time. Used on suspected informants, the "necklace" is a car tire, filled with petrol, put around the person's neck and set alight. The victims are mainly immigrants and refugees from other parts of Africa, including Zimbabwe, where a devastated economy has sent at least two million people across the border in search of a better life. Some say the attacks stem from a long-standing feeling among locals that the number of immigrants in South Africa results in shortages of jobs and essential needs. Inadequate housing, a lack of running water and electricity, the rising prices of food, and escalating crime -- nearly 20,000 people were slain in South Africa last year -- add to the resentment.  Watch analysis of reasons behind xenophobic attacks » . According to South Africa's latest census, the country has about 45 million people. The South African Department of Human Affairs estimates that more than 4 million people reside in South Africa illegally, but that figure is based on a 10-year-old study and some feel the number of immigrants in South Africa is much higher. Some say that millions have recently fled to South Africa from Zimbabwe because of violence there since the county's stalled election. A presidential run-off between long-time leader President Robert Mugabe and his opposition challenger, Morgan Tsvangirai, is scheduled for June 27 in Zimbabwe -- three months after the initial vote. Zimbabwe also is in the midst of an economic collapse, with nearly 80 percent unemployment.

Immigrants from Mozambique lined up in Primrose, South Africa, to board buses returning home. Overnight clashes left one person dead, led to 15 arrests, and prompted the evacuation of 420 foreign nationals, a Cape Town police official said.

“Crowds of people went on a rampage, looting and carrying out acts of violence,” said Cape Town Police Superintendent Billy Jones. Those arrested were charged with public violence and are scheduled to appear in court Monday.

One foreign national, a Somali, died after being run over by a vehicle while trying to escape the angry crowds, Jones said. Twelve people suffered minor injuries. He said Friday was tense but calm, with national and local police deployed throughout the area.

Jack Bloom of the opposition Democratic Alliance told CNN on Friday that government troops were assisting police in efforts to contain violence in Johannesburg. Aid workers and volunteers were providing tents, food, and other supplies at police stations. Bloom estimated that about 2,000 foreign nationals had sought refuge at those locations.

It was the first outbreak of violence in the coastal city since a wave of xenophobic attacks began about two weeks ago in Johannesburg, resulting in at least 42 deaths.

The foreign nationals were transported out of the city after angry crowds gathered at a public meeting intended to ease tensions, Jones told CNN. They were being housed in community centers and churches.

The attacks in South Africa have forced thousands of immigrants to flee, prompting neighboring Mozambique to declare a state of emergency on Friday. Desperate accounts emerged from those fleeing the violence.

Mozambique’s Foreign Minister Oldemiro Baloi said the decision was made after about 10,000 Mozambicans fled South Africa.

CNN’s Robyn Curnow reported long lines of people — many from Zimbabwe and Mozambique — waiting for buses in Johannesburg to take them home.

Bloom, from Gauteng province, which includes Johannesburg, said the attacks on foreigners who had fled to South Africa in search of a better life had become a “humanitarian crisis.”

South African President Thabo Mbeki has approved the deployment of the army to help stop the attacks, which have drawn condemnation from South African officials and other African leaders.

About 28,000 people have been displaced by the violence, said Hangwani Malaudzi, a spokesman for the Ministry of Safety and Security. More than 400 people have been arrested for crimes ranging from murder to causing a public disturbance, he said.

The country has also witnessed a disturbing return to the apartheid-era lynching tactic of the 1980s known as “necklacing,” which was widely used in the townships at the time. Used against suspected informants, the “necklace” is a car tire filled with petrol, placed around a person’s neck, and set alight.

The victims are mainly immigrants and refugees from other parts of Africa, including Zimbabwe, where a devastated economy has driven at least two million people across the border in search of a better life.

Some say the attacks stem from a long-standing belief among locals that the number of immigrants in South Africa has contributed to shortages of jobs and essential services. Inadequate housing, a lack of running water and electricity, rising food prices, and escalating crime — nearly 20,000 people were killed in South Africa last year — have added to the resentment.

According to South Africa’s latest census, the country has about 45 million people. A presidential run-off between longtime leader President Robert Mugabe and his opposition challenger, Morgan Tsvangirai, is scheduled for June 27 in Zimbabwe — three months after the initial vote.

Zimbabwe is also in the midst of an economic collapse, with unemployment at nearly 80 percent.

JOHANNESBURG, South Africa (CNN) — Tensions remained high in Cape Town on Friday after anti-immigrant violence that had already killed more than 40 people in Johannesburg reached South Africa’s largest city.

In Primrose, South Africa, Mozambican immigrants waited in lines to get on buses returning them to their country.

A Cape Town police official said overnight confrontations left one person dead, led to 15 arrests, and forced the evacuation of 420 foreign nationals.

Cape Town Police Superintendent Billy Jones said groups of people had gone through the area looting and committing violent acts. Those arrested were accused of public violence and were expected to appear in court on Monday.

Jones said a Somali foreign national was killed when he was struck by a vehicle while trying to flee the hostile crowds. Twelve others sustained minor injuries.

By Friday, Jones said, the situation was still strained but under control, with both national and local police deployed across the area.

Jack Bloom, a member of the opposition Democratic Alliance, told CNN on Friday that soldiers were assisting police in Johannesburg in efforts to contain the unrest. Relief workers and volunteers were delivering tents, food, and other necessities to police stations, where Bloom estimated roughly 2,000 foreign nationals had taken refuge.

The unrest marked the first outbreak of violence in the coastal city since xenophobic attacks began about two weeks earlier in Johannesburg, where at least 42 people had died.

Jones told CNN that foreign nationals were removed from the city after angry groups gathered during a public meeting intended to ease tensions. The evacuees were being sheltered in community centers and churches.

The violence in South Africa has driven thousands of immigrants from their homes and led neighboring Mozambique to announce a state of emergency on Friday.

Mozambican Foreign Minister Oldemiro Baloi said the move followed the flight of about 10,000 Mozambicans from South Africa.

CNN’s Robyn Curnow reported that long queues of people, including many Zimbabweans and Mozambicans, were waiting in Johannesburg for buses to take them back to their home countries.

Bloom, who is from Gauteng province, which includes Johannesburg, described the attacks on foreigners who had come to South Africa seeking better lives as a “humanitarian crisis.”

South African President Thabo Mbeki authorized the use of the military to help bring an end to the attacks, which have been denounced by South African authorities and leaders elsewhere in Africa.

Hangwani Malaudzi, a spokesman for the Ministry of Safety and Security, said approximately 28,000 people had been displaced. He added that more than 400 people had been arrested on charges ranging from murder to public disorder.

The violence has also included a troubling revival of “necklacing,” a lynching method associated with South Africa’s apartheid-era townships in the 1980s. The practice, once commonly used against suspected informants, involves placing a petrol-filled car tire around a person’s neck and setting it on fire.

Most of the victims are immigrants and refugees from elsewhere in Africa, including Zimbabwe. Zimbabwe’s economic devastation has pushed at least two million people across the border in search of improved living conditions.

Some observers say the violence is fueled by a long-running belief among some South Africans that immigration contributes to competition over jobs and basic services. Resentment has also been intensified by poor housing, shortages of running water and electricity, rising food costs, and worsening crime. Nearly 20,000 people were killed in South Africa last year.

South Africa’s most recent census put the country’s population at about 45 million. The South African Department of Human Affairs estimates that more than 4 million people are living in the country illegally, though that estimate is based on research that is a decade old, and some believe the true immigrant population is significantly larger.

Some people say millions have recently crossed into South Africa from Zimbabwe because of violence following Zimbabwe’s unresolved election. A presidential runoff between longtime President Robert Mugabe and opposition candidate Morgan Tsvangirai is set for June 27, three months after the first round of voting.

Zimbabwe is also experiencing severe economic collapse, with unemployment close to 80 percent.

# Xenophobic violence spreads from Johannesburg to Cape Town as South Africa deploys troops

**Cape Town, South Africa** — South Africa’s government has deployed troops to several urban areas after a wave of xenophobic violence that began in Johannesburg spread to Cape Town, leaving multiple people dead, dozens arrested and thousands of immigrants displaced, officials said.

Authorities said the unrest erupted earlier this week in parts of Johannesburg, where mobs attacked foreign-owned shops, torched vehicles and forced residents to flee their homes. By Friday, similar violence had been reported in neighborhoods around Cape Town, raising fears that the unrest was spreading across the country.

Police said at least **several people have been killed** in clashes and arson attacks, though officials warned the death toll could rise as emergency crews gain access to damaged buildings. More than **100 people have been arrested** on charges including public violence, looting, arson and assault, according to law enforcement officials.

The violence has primarily targeted immigrants from other African countries, including Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Malawi and Nigeria. Community groups said families have taken shelter in churches, police stations and temporary camps after fleeing attacks.

“This is not protest. This is criminality, and it will be dealt with decisively,” South Africa’s president said in a televised address, announcing the deployment of army units to support police in restoring order.

## Mozambique declares state of emergency

In neighboring Mozambique, officials declared a **state of emergency** along parts of the border and in areas receiving displaced citizens returning from South Africa.

Mozambican authorities said emergency shelters were being prepared for nationals fleeing the violence. The government also said it was coordinating with South African officials to evacuate vulnerable citizens and provide consular assistance.

“We are facing a humanitarian situation that requires immediate action,” a Mozambican government spokesperson said. “Our citizens must be protected, and those responsible for attacks must be held accountable.”

Buses carrying Mozambican nationals were seen arriving at border posts, where aid workers distributed food, blankets and medical supplies. Some returnees described hiding for days before escaping.

## Immigrant communities fearful

In Cape Town, foreign nationals said they were afraid to leave their homes after rumors circulated on social media calling for attacks on immigrant-owned businesses.

“I lost my shop in Johannesburg, then came here thinking I would be safe,” said one Malawian trader sheltering at a community center. “Now we are running again.”

Human rights organizations condemned the attacks and urged South African leaders to confront anti-immigrant rhetoric, unemployment and organized criminal exploitation.

South Africa has experienced repeated outbreaks of xenophobic violence over the past two decades, often fueled by frustration over jobs, housing and public services. Immigrants are frequently blamed for crime and economic hardship despite studies showing they make up a small portion of the population.

## Troops sent to hotspots

The South African National Defence Force said troops would be deployed in coordination with police to patrol affected areas, protect key infrastructure and prevent further looting.

Officials also announced additional security at taxi ranks, informal settlements and commercial districts where tensions remain high.

Opposition leaders called for calm but criticized the government for failing to respond quickly enough to early warnings.

“This violence did not come from nowhere,” one lawmaker said. “Communities have been warning authorities for months.”

As night fell in Cape Town and Johannesburg, police maintained a heavy presence in several neighborhoods. Authorities urged residents not to share inflammatory posts online and warned that anyone inciting violence would face prosecution.

“This country cannot allow hatred to define it,” the president said. “An attack on foreign nationals is an attack on South Africa’s values and its future.”

**BREAKING NEWS REPORT**  
**Date: 23 May 2008**  
**Location: Johannesburg / Cape Town, South Africa**

## Anti-Immigrant Violence Spreads Across South Africa as Thousands Flee Homes

South Africa is facing a deepening humanitarian crisis as violent attacks on foreign nationals continue to spread from Johannesburg to other parts of the country, including Cape Town, during the final months of President Thabo Mbeki’s administration.

The unrest, which began earlier this month in townships around Johannesburg, has left dozens dead, many more injured, and thousands displaced. Migrants from Mozambique and Zimbabwe are among those most heavily affected, with many saying they have been beaten, robbed, threatened, or forced to flee their homes by mobs accusing foreigners of taking jobs, housing, and public services.

Police have been deployed in several affected communities, and authorities say hundreds of people have been arrested in connection with murder, assault, looting, arson, and public violence. However, humanitarian groups warn that the state response has been slow and uneven, leaving frightened families crowded into police stations, community halls, churches, and makeshift shelters.

## Johannesburg Townships at the Centre of the Violence

The worst violence has been reported in and around Johannesburg, particularly in informal settlements and townships where poverty, unemployment, and overcrowded housing have fuelled local resentment.

Witnesses in areas including Alexandra, Diepsloot, Tembisa, and parts of the East Rand describe mobs moving through streets at night, demanding that foreign nationals leave. Homes and small shops belonging to migrants have been looted and set alight.

Several victims are reported to have been burned, beaten, or stabbed. Some South African residents have tried to protect their foreign neighbours, but others say fear of retaliation has kept them indoors.

Mozambican migrants, many of whom have lived in South Africa for years and work in construction, domestic service, informal trade, and security jobs, have been among the victims. Zimbabweans fleeing economic collapse and political violence in their own country have also been targeted.

A Zimbabwean man sheltering at a Johannesburg police station said he had fled Harare months earlier hoping to earn money for his family. “I came here because there is no work at home,” he said. “Now I have lost everything again. I do not know where I can go.”

## Cape Town Communities on Edge

Violence and intimidation have now been reported in parts of Cape Town, raising fears that the attacks are spreading nationally. Police and city officials have confirmed that foreign nationals have fled homes in several communities after threats and assaults.

In areas around Cape Town’s townships and informal settlements, including parts of Khayelitsha, Philippi, and Du Noon, migrants have sought refuge in police stations, churches, municipal buildings, and temporary safety sites.

Local aid workers say many of the displaced in Cape Town are Zimbabwean, Mozambican, Malawian, Somali, and Congolese nationals. Some families fled with only the clothes they were wearing, leaving behind identity documents, savings, school uniforms, and household possessions.

Authorities in the Western Cape say contingency plans are being activated to accommodate displaced people, though aid organisations warn that food, blankets, sanitation, and medical support are urgently needed.

## Police Response Intensifies

The South African Police Service has increased patrols in affected areas, with officers using rubber bullets, tear gas, and mass arrests in some locations to disperse violent crowds. Police officials say they are working to restore order and prevent further attacks.

National and provincial authorities have condemned the violence, describing it as criminal and unacceptable. President Mbeki’s government has appealed for calm and called on communities not to target foreign nationals.

Security officials say special attention is being given to informal settlements where tensions remain high. However, critics argue that police intervention has often come only after homes and shops have already been destroyed.

Human rights organisations have called for stronger protection of migrants and refugees, saying many victims are reluctant to report attacks because they fear detention, deportation, or further victimisation.

## Humanitarian Impact Worsens

The attacks have created one of the most serious displacement crises South Africa has faced since the end of apartheid. Thousands of foreign nationals and some South Africans accused of protecting them are now living in overcrowded shelters.

Medical workers report treating victims for burns, stab wounds, broken bones, and severe trauma. Children have been separated from parents in the chaos, while pregnant women, elderly people, and people living with chronic illnesses face particular risks.

Aid agencies say the humanitarian needs are growing rapidly:

- **Emergency shelter** for families fleeing violence  
- **Food and clean water** at police stations and temporary camps  
- **Medical care** for injured and traumatised victims  
- **Protection for children** and other vulnerable groups  
- **Assistance with lost documents** and access to asylum procedures  
- **Safe transport** for those wishing to return home or relocate  

Some Mozambican nationals are reportedly considering returning across the border, despite having built lives in South Africa over many years. Zimbabweans face a more uncertain choice, with many saying they cannot return safely because of economic hardship and political instability at home.

## Anger Rooted in Poverty and Competition

Community leaders say the violence has been fuelled by a combination of poverty, unemployment, housing shortages, and frustration with local service delivery. Foreign nationals are being blamed for social problems that many analysts say are rooted in deeper economic inequality.

South Africa has long attracted migrants from across southern Africa, particularly from Mozambique and Zimbabwe. Many enter the country seeking work, safety, or access to basic services. But in poor communities, competition for jobs, housing, and trading space has contributed to rising tension.

Anti-immigrant sentiment has been growing for years, with foreign nationals often accused—without evidence—of causing crime or undercutting wages. Rights groups say the current violence reflects both social desperation and a failure by political leaders to confront xenophobia before it escalated.

## Government Under Pressure

The Mbeki administration is under increasing pressure to act decisively. Opposition parties, civil society groups, churches, and migrant-rights organisations are calling for stronger security measures and urgent humanitarian assistance.

There are also calls for senior government officials to visit affected communities, publicly reject xenophobia, and reassure migrants that they are entitled to protection under South African law.

International attention is growing, particularly from neighbouring countries whose citizens have been attacked. Mozambique and Zimbabwe are expected to monitor the situation closely, while diplomatic officials may seek guarantees for the safety of their nationals.

## Fear Remains Despite Police Presence

Although police patrols have restored calm in some areas, fear remains widespread. Many migrants say they do not trust that they can return home safely. In several communities, foreign-owned shops remain closed, streets are tense, and rumours of further attacks continue to circulate.

A Mozambican woman sheltering with her children in Cape Town said she had lived in South Africa for nearly a decade. “My children go to school here,” she said. “This is the only home they know. But now people tell us we must leave.”

Humanitarian organisations warn that unless the violence is contained quickly and displaced families are protected, the crisis could worsen in the coming days.

For now, South Africa faces a severe test of public order, social cohesion, and its post-apartheid commitment to human rights as thousands of migrants wait in fear, uncertain whether they will be able to return to their homes—or whether they still have homes to return to.

**South Africa Struggles to Contain Xenophobic Violence as Attacks Spread**

**JOHANNESBURG/CAPE TOWN, South Africa —** South African authorities moved to restore order after a wave of xenophobic violence swept through townships and informal settlements in 2008, leaving dozens dead, thousands displaced and exposing deep tensions over poverty, unemployment and migration.

The attacks, which began in the Johannesburg area before spreading to other parts of the country, targeted foreign nationals accused by some residents of taking jobs, housing and business opportunities. Victims included migrants from Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Somalia and other African countries, many of whom had come to South Africa seeking work, safety or better living conditions.

In Cape Town, clashes broke out in several communities as groups of residents attacked foreign-owned shops and homes. Police were deployed to contain unrest, while community leaders and officials appealed for calm. Somali shopkeepers were among those targeted, with businesses looted or burned in some areas. Mozambican migrants were also reported among the victims of assaults elsewhere in the country.

Thousands of foreign nationals fled their homes and sought shelter at police stations, community halls, churches and temporary camps. Many said they were too afraid to return, even after police increased patrols. Families slept in crowded conditions with few possessions, relying on aid groups for blankets, food and medical care.

Police said hundreds of people were arrested in connection with murder, assault, robbery, arson and public violence. Authorities condemned the attacks and vowed to prosecute those responsible. Officials also expressed alarm over reports of “necklacing,” a brutal form of killing associated with South Africa’s apartheid-era political violence, in which victims are set alight with a tire placed around the body.

The violence shocked many South Africans, coming years after the end of apartheid and amid the country’s effort to present itself as a stable democracy and regional leader. President Thabo Mbeki’s government faced criticism over its response, with opponents and civil society groups saying the state had failed to address anti-immigrant sentiment and the conditions that fueled it.

The unrest also unfolded against the backdrop of political and economic crisis in neighboring Zimbabwe. Years of economic collapse, food shortages and political repression had driven large numbers of Zimbabweans into South Africa. In 2008, Zimbabwe was in turmoil following disputed elections and a tense confrontation between President Robert Mugabe and opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai, adding to the flow of migrants across the border.

Analysts said the violence reflected a volatile mix of local grievances and scapegoating. South Africa’s poorest communities faced overcrowding, high unemployment and inadequate public services, while migrants became easy targets for frustration.

Human rights groups urged the government to protect displaced people and combat xenophobia more aggressively. Religious leaders, trade unions and community organizations called for reconciliation, warning that the attacks undermined South Africa’s post-apartheid commitment to human rights and African solidarity.

For many survivors, however, the immediate concern was safety. “We came here because we thought South Africa was a place of peace,” one displaced foreign national said at a temporary shelter. “Now we do not know where to go.”

JOHANNESBURG, South Africa (CNN) -- Xenophobic violence sweeping parts of South Africa has killed more than 40 people and driven thousands of African immigrants from their homes, forcing many to seek shelter in police stations, churches and makeshift camps, officials and aid workers said.

The attacks, which began in townships around Johannesburg and later spread to other areas, have targeted migrants from neighboring countries including Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Malawi and Somalia. Witnesses described mobs armed with sticks, knives and clubs attacking foreign-owned shops, burning homes and accusing immigrants of taking jobs and housing.

South African police said they had arrested hundreds of people in connection with the unrest, including suspects accused of murder, assault, arson and looting. Authorities have deployed additional officers and, in some areas, soldiers to help restore order.

President Thabo Mbeki condemned the attacks, calling on South Africans to reject violence against foreign nationals and warning that the unrest threatened the country’s democratic values.

Many of those fleeing the violence said they no longer felt safe in South Africa, which has long attracted migrants seeking work and refuge from political and economic crises elsewhere on the continent.

Humanitarian groups said displaced families were in urgent need of food, blankets, medical care and sanitation. Aid workers warned that overcrowded shelters could lead to further health and security problems if the violence continues.

The unrest has exposed deep frustration in South Africa’s poorest communities, where unemployment, poverty and housing shortages remain widespread more than a decade after the end of apartheid. Analysts say immigrants have become scapegoats for economic hardship, despite contributing to local economies.

South Africa’s government has pledged to protect foreign nationals and prosecute those responsible for the attacks, but many displaced migrants said they were considering returning to their home countries rather than risk further violence.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an article summarizing the spread of xenophobic attacks in South Africa, with quotes from police and opposition officials, statistics on deaths and displacement, aid efforts, causes such as unemployment and housing shortages, and background on Zimbabwean migration.
counterfactuals.output:
## Xenophobic Violence Spreads Across South Africa, Leaving Dozens Dead and Thousands Displaced

Xenophobic attacks that began in Johannesburg’s townships spread across parts of South Africa, leaving scores of people dead, forcing thousands from their homes and exposing deep tensions over poverty, unemployment, housing shortages and immigration.

The violence, directed mainly at foreign African migrants, erupted in May 2008 in the township of Alexandra, north of Johannesburg, before spreading to other areas of Gauteng province and then to cities including Durban and Cape Town. Mobs attacked immigrants from Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Malawi, Somalia and other African countries, accusing them of taking jobs, housing and business opportunities from South Africans.

Police said they were struggling to contain scattered outbreaks of violence as residents were beaten, homes were looted and burned, and makeshift camps formed around police stations, churches and community halls.

“We are doing everything possible to restore order and protect people who have been targeted,” police officials said at the time, while confirming arrests linked to murder, assault, arson and public violence.

By the time the worst of the attacks subsided, at least 60 people had been killed, including South Africans mistakenly identified as foreigners. Tens of thousands more were displaced, with many sheltering in temporary camps or fleeing back to their countries of origin. Humanitarian groups estimated that more than 100,000 people were uprooted during the crisis.

Opposition leaders accused the government of failing to respond quickly enough to warnings of growing hostility toward migrants.

“This did not happen overnight,” opposition officials said, arguing that the attacks reflected a breakdown in local governance and years of unmet promises on jobs, housing and public services.

Aid organizations, churches and local volunteers moved to provide emergency food, blankets, medical care and shelter. The South African Red Cross, Médecins Sans Frontières, faith groups and community organizations helped set up relief sites for displaced families. The government also deployed police and, in some areas, the army to help restore order.

The attacks highlighted the pressures facing South Africa’s poorest communities. Many residents in informal settlements were already competing for scarce jobs and limited housing. High unemployment, rising food prices and slow delivery of basic services created fertile ground for resentment. Foreign migrants, often willing to accept low-paid work or operate small informal businesses, became convenient scapegoats.

Zimbabwean migrants were among the largest groups affected. Years of political turmoil, economic collapse and hyperinflation in Zimbabwe had driven millions to seek work and safety in South Africa. Estimates at the time varied widely, but many analysts believed that between one million and three million Zimbabweans were living in South Africa, many without formal documentation.

While South Africa has long been a destination for migrants from across the continent, the 2008 attacks shocked the country and the region. They also challenged South Africa’s post-apartheid image as a refuge for Africans fleeing conflict and economic hardship elsewhere.

Government officials condemned the violence as criminal and un-African, insisting that migrants had a right to protection. But activists warned that unless the underlying causes — poverty, unemployment, housing shortages, weak policing and anti-immigrant rhetoric — were addressed, xenophobic violence could return.

In the years since, South Africa has continued to experience periodic outbreaks of anti-foreigner violence, especially in poor urban areas. The 2008 attacks remain one of the clearest warnings of how economic desperation and political neglect can turn communities against some of their most vulnerable residents.
